Compared with related instruments, the hand-sock cymbal is mounted on a spring scissors clamp and the player squeezes the clamp to bring the cymbals together; the squash cymbal is mounted on simple tongs, held in one hand and struck with a drumstick in the other. Its way of sounding is unlike that of the pedal-operated hi-hat.
手持響鈸的前身是路德威格拉德斯通鈸，由比利格拉德斯通發明、路德威鼓公司生產。該公: The bock-a-da-bock's forerunner was the Ludwig Gladstone cymbal, invented by Billy Gladstone and made by the Ludwig Drum Company. That company and its competitors developed the design further into several hand-held cymbals, and the bock-a-da-bock is listed in the Ludwig Drum Company catalogue of 1928. Because of the limits of 1920s recording it was used in place of the trap set; after the trap set turned into the modern drum kit in the 1930s it gradually lost players' favour, being less useful than the pedal-operated hi-hat.

The bock-a-da-bock is a percussion instrument made of two small cymbals joined by a metal clamp. It is usually played by one percussionist holding a pair in one hand and striking them like castanets. It is listed as a product in the 1928 Ludwig Drum Company catalogue and, because of the limits of 1920s recording, was once used as a substitute for the trap set. On jazz recordings, Kaiser Marshall played it on Fletcher Henderson records, and Zutty Singleton used it on Louis Armstrong's Hot Five recordings.
演奏者通常將兩組小型鈸分持於左右手，像響板一樣成對使用，使每組中的兩個小鈸相互碰: The player usually holds a pair of small cymbals in each hand and uses them as castanets, so that the two cymbals in each pair strike each other; this differs from the squash cymbal, which is struck with a drumstick, and from the hand-sock cymbal, where the clamp is squeezed. A beginner can first hold one pair steadily in one hand, then add the other hand playing alternately.
